title: Let me convince you to try writing a script
author: Alex Blanksby
summary: Alex Blanksby makes the case for lesson scripting by reframing what a script actually is: not a 60-minute monologue but a collection of short, modular 5-second to 2-minute chunks that can be re-sequenced, inserted, and rebuilt as a lesson unfolds. Scripts reduce the extraneous cognitive load of deciding how to phrase things in real time, letting teachers focus cognitive resources on what students are doing rather than what they should say next. He argues that scripts can be personalized: just as musicians and actors interpret the same written material differently, two teachers can deliver the same script with entirely different energy, pace, and personality. A key practical benefit is consistency in question phrasing when building student fluency—the same sentence structure, asked the same way dozens of times, reduces processing overhead and increases repetitions per class period. Blanksby notes that teachers have very few opportunities to refine an introduction to a given concept across a year, making pre-written, tested scripts a way to outsource that refinement work to a quieter moment outside the classroom. The post closes with a practical exercise: write a 2-minute script for a concept you're teaching next week, destroy it, then rewrite it from memory—using what you learned from the first attempt.
points: A lesson script is not a 60-minute monologue but a collection of modular 5-second to 2-minute chunks that can be sequenced, re-sequenced, removed, and rebuilt in response to how students respond—giving flexibility rather than constraining it.

Scripts reduce extraneous cognitive load by pre-resolving how to say things, freeing the teacher's working memory during instruction to focus on student responses rather than phrasing—and making question prompts shorter, snappier, and more repeatable.

The musician and actor analogy: just as two performers interpret the same score or script with different energy, timing, and personality, two teachers can deliver the same instructional script in ways that are distinctive—nowhere in the script does it say to deliver it with zero enthusiasm.
quotes: When I am talking about a script, I am not talking about a full 60-minute run down of an entire lesson as a singular fixed script. I am generally talking about much, much shorter scripts that might last 5 seconds to a minute or two.
What learning scripts can do is minimise the extraneous cognitive load of deciding how to say what comes next.
One of the biggest uses I have for scripts is to minimise the variation in the wording of my questions and prompts to students when building fluency.

Does a musician write the score of every piece they play? No. Maybe they compose some pieces, but they will play a large number of pieces from other composers. Does that mean that the same piece played by different musicians will sound exactly the same? No. They put their own interpretation into it.
How many times have you actually, out loud, gone through an explanation of a particular concept? No, seriously. Think about one in particular and try and work out a rough estimate.
We can test out different variations of sentence structures and wording choices. We can test which examples, metaphors, or analogies appear to be more or less effective.
